network.overall_strategy: This is a literature-constrained candidate synthesis network, not an experimentally completed synthesis or a claim that ten validated prebiotic routes exist. Ten distinct reaction sequences are enumerated: eight variants of the cyanosulfidic scaffold and two independently sourced ornithine routes. The eight scaffold variants test chemically relevant differences in guanidination timing, copper availability during the first photoreduction, and terminal hydrolysis conditions; they are not eight independent discoveries. Patel et al. (2015) provide the strongest evidence through the arginine alpha-aminonitrile, not quantitatively recovered free arginine. Neither selective endpoint hydrolysis nor environmental free-ornithine guanidination is established by the supplied evidence. All numerical operating windows below are proposed experimental screening conditions unless explicitly identified as reported observations; missing literature protocols, rates, yields, and transport recoveries are not invented. Sequential reagent delivery is essential. For every transfer, downstream concentration must be calculated as recovered moles divided by receiving volume, with recovery measured rather than assumed quantitative. No overall yield can presently be assigned. Neutral parent formulas are used consistently; actual protonation depends on pH. S8 is an idealized terminal sulfur balance product, not an assertion that it is the primary photoproduct. Non-target sink species use the schema's intermediate role because no byproduct role is available. environment_formed identifies a representative formation setting, not an exclusive one. All stages are anoxic, no enzyme or molecular oxygen is invoked, and no stereoselective production of L-arginine is claimed.

reactions.name: Copper-mediated hydrocyanation of acetylene
agents: Cu(I) coordinated by chloride and cyanide

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm, with a replenished gas-water interface
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 6-8; total dissolved cyanide 1-30 mM; dissolved acetylene 0.1-10 mM; total copper 0.01-0.1 mM; 1-72 h. Exclude sulfide from this inlet because copper sulfide precipitation can disable the catalyst. Measure dissolved copper speciation, volatile-feedstock loss, and acrylonitrile production rather than assuming quantitative capture.

reactions.mechanism: Cu(I)-mediated addition of HCN across acetylene produces acrylonitrile; this is hydrocyanation, not an oxygen-dependent oxidative coupling.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support the HCN/acetylene entry to the acrylonitrile branch. The supplied report does not establish the numerical operating window used here, which is a proposed screen. Concentrated cyanide supply remains conditional: Toner and Catling (2019) support geological storage and concentration mechanisms, not this complete downstream reaction sequence.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9-10; acrylonitrile 1-10 mM; total ammonia/ammonium 0.1-0.5 M; 1-72 h. The ammonia excess is intended to reduce multiple cyanoethylation but is a substantial local concentration requirement. Quantify secondary-amine products and acrylonitrile loss.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia undergoes conjugate addition to the activated alkene, followed by proton transfer, producing 3-aminopropanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This transformation is part of the experimentally developed arginine/proline precursor network of Patel et al. (2015). The proposed concentration and residence-time ranges are not recovered experimental conditions from that paper. Product selectivity must be measured because the first-formed amine can also react with acrylonitrile.

reactions.name: Copper-assisted photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; aminonitrile 1-10 mM; total dissolved sulfide 1-10 mM, supplied incrementally; total copper 0.01-0.1 mM; irradiated water depth 1-5 mm. Laboratory comparison: 254 nm, measured incident irradiance 0.05-0.5 mW/cm2, sampled over 1-24 h. Cyanamide trapping must occur during aldehyde generation rather than after storage of the unstable aldehyde. Determine photoactive copper remaining after sulfide and Fe2+ precipitation reactions.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-supported photoredox reduction of the nitrile gives an imine-equivalent, whose hydrolysis releases ammonia and 3-aminopropanal. Sulfur oxidation supplies the formal reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support the nitrile-to-aldehyde chemistry and subsequent cyanamide interception. The irradiation and solution ranges here are proposed tests, not claimed reproduction conditions. Ranjan et al. (2018) show why millimolar sulfide cannot be assumed in generic surface waters, while Ranjan and Sasselov (2017) support surface UV availability without establishing this substrate's environmental action spectrum.

reactions.name: Aldehyde-stage cyanamide trapping and cyclic hemiaminal formation

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; cyanamide 5-50 mM; aldehyde generated in situ from a 0.1-5 mM precursor pool. Sample from minutes to 24 h. Deliver cyanamide before or during aldehyde photogeneration, with no assumed isolation of free 3-aminopropanal. Measure cyanamide depletion and competing cyclic or oligomeric products.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanamide intercepts the aminoaldehyde through coupled addition and intramolecular guanidine-forming chemistry. The guanidinated aldehyde is represented by its cyclic hemiaminal, 2-imino-1,3-diazinan-4-ol.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identify efficient aldehyde-stage interception as the productive improvement over relatively inefficient direct aminonitrile guanidination. The explicit cyclic species prevents treating an unstable open-chain aldehyde as a persistent reservoir. Formation and ring-opening flux still require measurement under the proposed environmental conditions.

reactions.name: Early guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10.5; aminonitrile 1-10 mM; cyanamide 10-100 mM; 0.5-48 h before irradiation. Quantify the guanidinated nitrile directly. Residual cyanamide and unreacted aminonitrile must be tracked separately because they can enter the aldehyde-trapping route.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal primary amine attacks cyanamide's electrophilic carbon, followed by proton transfers and tautomerization to an N-substituted guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report this guanidination as relatively inefficient. It is retained as a chemically distinct minor entry, not as an equally productive substitute for aldehyde-stage trapping. Product recovered after irradiating an unseparated mixture cannot be assigned entirely to this edge.

reactions.name: Copper-assisted photoreduction of the early-guanylated nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; guanidinated nitrile 0.1-5 mM; total sulfide 1-10 mM; total copper 0.01-0.1 mM; 1-5 mm optical path; 254 nm laboratory irradiation at measured 0.05-0.5 mW/cm2 for 1-24 h. Use analytical separation or tracer-resolved experiments to distinguish this flux from reduction of residual unguanidinated nitrile; natural purification is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile photoreduction and imine hydrolysis generate a guanidinated propanal, which cyclizes to the same hemiaminal reached by aldehyde-stage trapping.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) motivate this connected branch, but the supplied report does not establish an isolated-substrate yield for this particular channel. Its quantitative contribution is therefore unresolved, especially when residual cyanamide permits the competing aldehyde-trapping sequence. Copper and sulfide speciation impose the same limitations as in rxn_003.

reactions.name: Candidate copper-free sulfide photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; aminonitrile 0.1-5 mM; total dissolved sulfide 1-20 mM; 1-5 mm optical path; measured 254 nm irradiance 0.05-0.5 mW/cm2; 1-48 h. Entry-stage copper must have been retained or precipitated upstream; residual dissolved copper must be measured. Cyanamide is present for immediate downstream trapping. This is not a copper-free acetylene-entry pathway.

reactions.mechanism: UV excitation of sulfide is hypothesized to supply reducing equivalents without copper mediation, followed by nitrile reduction and hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific alternative. Patel et al. (2015) support copper-independent sulfide photochemistry in parts of the broader network, but the supplied findings do not establish useful conversion of this substrate without copper. The alternative is motivated by copper sequestration, not by demonstrated equal performance. Ranjan et al. (2018) constrain the required sulfide supply.

reactions.name: Candidate copper-free sulfide photoreduction of the early-guanylated nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; guanidinated nitrile 0.1-5 mM; total sulfide 1-20 mM; 254 nm laboratory irradiation at measured 0.05-0.5 mW/cm2 over 1-48 h. Verify low dissolved copper and distinguish conversion of the guanidinated substrate from residual beta-aminopropionitrile. Determine whether guanidinium protonation changes reduction selectivity.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized sulfide-only photoreduction converts the nitrile to an aldehyde equivalent, followed by intramolecular hemiaminal formation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative: neither general copper-free photochemistry nor conservation of atoms establishes this substrate-specific edge. Patel et al. (2015) provide only the broader chemical motivation in the supplied evidence. This branch compounds inefficient early guanidination with an unvalidated reduction and must not be ranked alongside the strongest scaffold without measurements.

reactions.name: First carbon homologation by cyanide capture of the guanidinated aldehyde equivalent

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; hemiaminal 0.1-10 mM; total cyanide 5-50 mM; 0.5-24 h. Add cyanide after the preceding reduction stage. Lower free ammonia relative to the final Strecker stage so that cyanohydrin capture can compete with aminonitrile formation. Measure volatile HCN loss and ring-open versus cyclic species.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible hemiaminal ring opening exposes the aldehyde, and cyanide addition traps it as 4-(carbamimidamido)-2-hydroxybutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This homologation follows the guanidinated branch described by Patel et al. (2015). Ring opening is coupled to capture rather than represented as a quantitatively accumulated free aldehyde. Cyanide concentration and reagent sequencing remain environmental requirements, not consequences of graph connectivity.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition to the homologation-stage nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8-9.5; cyanohydrin 0.1-10 mM; total sulfide 5-30 mM; dark or mineral-shaded incubation for 1-48 h before the next irradiation. Determine dissolved sulfide after FeS precipitation, not merely the amount added. Sulfur is incorporated into the substrate here.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrosulfide adds to the nitrile carbon, and proton transfers produce the alpha-hydroxythioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support the alpha-hydroxythioamide homologation sequence. Sulfide is a reactant rather than a decorative mineral agent, and sulfite cannot replace it merely by providing electrons. Ranjan et al. (2018) make local dissolved-sulfide availability a significant bottleneck.

reactions.name: Photochemical deoxygenation of the alpha-hydroxythioamide

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; hydroxythioamide 0.1-5 mM; dissolved sulfide 1-10 mM; total copper 0.01-0.1 mM; 1-5 mm optical path. Use measured 254 nm irradiation at 0.05-0.5 mW/cm2, sampling over 1-24 h. Quantify deoxygenated thioamide separately from decomposition products and monitor sulfur precipitation that could attenuate UV.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-supported photochemistry replaces the alpha-hydroxyl group with hydrogen, preserving the thioamide needed for the next homologation stage.
reactions.reasoning: The reaction class and its position in the arginine precursor sequence follow Patel et al. (2015). The proposed copper loading and photochemical dose are screening variables, not established environmental optima. S8 closes an idealized electron and atom balance; actual sulfur products, optical attenuation, and reductant consumption require measurement.

reactions.name: Thioamide photoreduction and hydrolysis to the elongated aldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; thioamide 0.1-5 mM; maintained sulfide bath 1-10 mM; total copper 0.01-0.1 mM; 254 nm at measured 0.05-0.5 mW/cm2 for 1-24 h. Capture the generated aldehyde promptly in the next stage. H2S occurs on both sides only to identify the required sulfide-containing medium; its cancellation does not establish recovery or catalytic turnover. Measure dissolved sulfide, polysulfides, solid sulfur, and ammonia.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical reduction/desulfurization and subsequent hydrolysis furnish 4-(carbamimidamido)butanal. The displayed net channel idealizes the sulfur products rather than specifying every photochemical elementary step.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support further processing of the homologation-stage thioamide toward the arginine precursor. The formal balanced channel cannot determine actual sulfur speciation or electron-transfer turnover. This distinction is necessary because a sulfide-containing photochemical bath is not equivalent to a proven recyclable H2S catalyst.

reactions.name: Second cyanide homologation to the arginine-skeleton cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9; aldehyde generated at 0.1-5 mM; total cyanide 5-50 mM; 0.5-24 h. Deliver cyanide promptly after aldehyde formation. Postpone the large ammonia addition until the final aminonitrile-forming stage, and measure carbonyl trapping versus aldehyde loss.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, adding the carbon that will become the amino acid carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: This carbon-extension logic is part of the experimentally supported precursor scaffold of Patel et al. (2015). The product has a five-carbon amino-acid backbone plus the separate guanidino carbon. A connected sequence does not establish that transient aldehyde survives transfer at useful concentration.

reactions.name: Strecker-type conversion of the cyanohydrin to arginine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9-10.5; cyanohydrin 0.1-5 mM; total ammonia/ammonium 0.05-0.5 M; residual cyanide maintained and measured; 1-48 h in a shaded aqueous compartment. Confirm the aminonitrile structure rather than assigning it from nominal mass alone. No chiral catalyst or enantiomer enrichment is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation, aldehyde-imine formation with ammonia, and cyanide capture produce the alpha-aminonitrile. This is not assumed to be direct substitution of an unactivated hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identify compound 46 as the arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor. This is the strongest experimentally supported arginine-specific endpoint in the supplied de novo sequence. Neither its identification nor the proposed conditions demonstrate quantitative conversion to free arginine.

reactions.name: Candidate acid-promoted hydration of arginine alpha-aminonitrile
agents: Hydronium supplied by HCl-bearing volcanic fluids

conditions.other: Proposed screen, not an established endpoint protocol: cooled-sample pH 0.5-2; aminonitrile 0.1-10 mM; sample from 6 h to 30 days. Use a dark, shallow subsurface acidic compartment downstream of the UV chemistry. HCl-derived acidity avoids requiring molecular oxygen. Quantify dilution and recovery during transfer, aminonitrile decomposition, amide formation, and guanidino-group retention.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation facilitates water addition and proton transfers, giving argininamide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a substrate-specific prebiotic operating step. Ordinary nitrile hydrolysis supplies chemical precedent, but Patel et al. (2015) do not establish free-arginine recovery under this proposed window. This explicitly resolves the otherwise hidden terminal-hydrolysis assumption into a testable bottleneck; no conversion or residence-time sufficiency is claimed.

reactions.name: Candidate acid-promoted argininamide hydrolysis to free arginine
agents: Hydronium supplied by HCl-bearing volcanic fluids

conditions.other: Proposed screen: cooled-sample pH 0.5-2; argininamide 0.1-10 mM; 6 h to 30 days, with time-resolved sampling rather than a presumed completion time. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium under these conditions. Determine free arginine by isotope-dilution chromatography with authentic standards, and use structural discrimination against constitutional isomers. Cool and dilute samples promptly for product-stability assessment.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted addition of water to the amide carbonyl and C-N cleavage form the carboxylic acid and ammonium, represented using neutral parent formulas.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative under the stated geological conditions: amide hydrolysis is conventional chemistry, but the supplied literature contains no validated argininamide-to-arginine protocol with substrate-specific yield and survival in this window. Patel et al. (2015) must not be cited as having completed this endpoint. This step is accepted only if measured arginine accumulation exceeds concurrent destruction.

reactions.name: Candidate alkaline hydrothermal hydration of arginine alpha-aminonitrile
agents: Hydroxide maintained by alkaline water-rock interaction

conditions.other: Proposed screen: cooled-sample pH 10-11.5; aminonitrile 0.1-10 mM; 1-90 days in a dark alkaline fluid compartment. The in situ temperature-dependent pH must also be determined. Transport from the surface requires an explicitly measured recovery and receiving volume. Quantify nitrile hydration, deamination, guanidino loss, and total organic-carbon recovery.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-assisted attack on the nitrile, followed by proton transfers, is hypothesized to yield the amide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative alternative motivated by naturally alkaline water-rock systems, not a demonstrated arginine pathway. Neither Patel et al. (2015) nor Kaur et al. (2024) establish this endpoint: Kaur et al. support different reductive-amination chemistry. A plausible pH setting does not establish an acceptable hydration rate or preservation of this substrate.

reactions.name: Candidate alkaline argininamide hydrolysis
agents: Hydroxide maintained by alkaline water-rock interaction

conditions.other: Proposed screen: cooled-sample pH 10-11.5; argininamide 0.1-10 mM; time-resolved sampling over 1-90 days. Maintain and measure alkalinity because amide hydrolysis changes proton inventories. Quantify arginine, ornithine, urea, and unidentified products. The chosen duration is a screening limit, not a prediction of completion.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide addition to the amide carbonyl and collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate produce carboxylate and ammonia; neutral parent formulas are displayed.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific endpoint with no direct support in the supplied studies. It tests whether geological alkalinity can substitute for an acidic finishing stage, but is not presumed superior. Concurrent guanidino hydrolysis and other degradation can prevent accumulation even when amide cleavage occurs; Kaur et al. (2024) do not resolve this missing arginine chemistry.

reactions.name: Lumped volcanic-discharge source channel for ornithine

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K in the aqueous collector; electrical discharge is a nonequilibrium energy source
conditions.other: Proposed source analogue: methane/ammonia-rich gas contacting anoxic water mist and intermittent electrical discharges, with collection over 1-7 days. Gas mixing ratios, electrical energy input, and collected organic concentrations must be measured rather than inferred from this net equation. Analyze free ornithine separately from ornithine released only by analytical hydrolysis. Concentration before guanidination requires a measured rainout and evaporation balance.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained product channel through discharge-generated carbonyl, cyanide, and nitrogenous mixtures, including hydrolysis of precursor material where applicable. It is not an elementary or selective methane-to-ornithine reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Johnson et al. (2008), together with the subsequent ornithine evidence described in the supplied report, support volcanic-discharge material as an abiotic ornithine source. They do not establish the displayed net channel as a selective mechanism or demonstrate delivery of sufficient free ornithine to cyanamide. Unidentified intermediates and the broad product mixture are deliberately not replaced by invented elementary steps.

reactions.name: Lumped heterogeneous CO/H2/NH3 source channel for ornithine
agents: Metallic nickel at a gas-solid interface

conditions.temperature: 500-600 K for the proposed hot interface, followed by rapid cooling for collection
conditions.pressure: Proposed 10-50 bar; not an experimentally established pressure window for this product
conditions.other: Hypothetical gas-dominated subsurface pore, not an ordinary aqueous vent. Screen CO/H2/NH3 feeds over 1 h to 7 days while measuring gas composition; keep water activity low enough to maintain the gas-solid stage. Sulfide must be low because it can poison nickel. Cool products to 300-330 K before aqueous extraction and separately quantify any hydrolysis required to release ornithine. Report catalyst state, collection recovery, free-versus-bound ornithine, and mixture-wide carbon balance.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained heterogeneous carbon-chain growth and nitrogen incorporation produce a complex organic mixture from which ornithine or hydrolyzable ornithine precursors may be recovered. No unique intermediate sequence is established.
reactions.reasoning: Yoshino et al. (1971) reported amino acids from CO/H2/NH3 over heterogeneous catalysts at 473-973 K; Hayatsu, Studier and Anders (1971) included ornithine in their isotope/MS-confirmed products. That evidence supports ornithine provenance, not this proposed narrower temperature-pressure window or selective production. Their failure to confirm arginine is respected: there is no direct FTT-to-arginine edge. The hydrothermal gas-pore placement and cooling/workup sequence remain geochemical extrapolations.

reactions.name: Candidate delta-selective guanidination of free ornithine by cyanamide

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10.5; free ornithine 0.1-10 mM; cyanamide 5-100 mM; 1-14 days. Use shaded concentrated water rather than assuming beneficial dry-down. Measure both amine-site products, cyanamide hydrolysis, dimerization, and ornithine lactamization. Resolve arginine from N-alpha-guanylornithine by chromatography with authentic standards and structural spectroscopy; exact mass alone cannot distinguish them.

reactions.mechanism: The ornithine delta-amine attacks cyanamide, installing the guanidino carbon and two additional nitrogens. The alpha-amine remains a competing nucleophile.
reactions.reasoning: Longo et al. (2020) establish the chemical concept of ornithine-to-arginine conversion and demonstrate it on model polypeptides, but their quantitative experiment is not a free-ornithine/cyanamide pond simulation. This free-monomer edge is therefore a candidate, not a demonstrated selective protocol. pH alone does not guarantee delta selectivity because the alpha-amine is more readily deprotonated. Cyanamide competition and the independent cost of ornithine supply remain central bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Competing cyanamide hydrolysis to urea

conditions.other: Proposed sink measurements: pH 5-10.5; cyanamide 1-100 mM; monitor from hours to weeks in the same matrices used for productive guanidination. Determine temperature- and pH-dependent disappearance rather than assuming either instantaneous hydrolysis or indefinite stability.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to the cyanamide nitrile functionality and proton transfers produce urea.
reactions.reasoning: Steinman, Lemmon and Calvin (1964) support cyanamide's aqueous prebiotic reactivity, while the supplied research emphasizes the competition between persistence and hydrolysis. That work does not provide a rate law for the present mixed matrices. This sink is included to prevent allocating the same cyanamide inventory independently to every productive pathway.

reactions.name: Competing cyanamide dimerization

conditions.other: Proposed sink screen: pH 8-10.5; cyanamide 10-100 mM before further evaporation; hours to weeks. Measure the changing water volume during concentration. The reaction consumes two cyanamide equivalents, represented by a single input ID as required by the schema.

reactions.mechanism: Intermolecular addition of cyanamide to cyanamide, followed by proton transfers, produces 2-cyanoguanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically established cyanamide self-reaction, but its flux in this particular network is unvalidated. The supplied research explicitly identifies dicyandiamide production as a necessary competing measurement; Steinman, Lemmon and Calvin (1964) do not establish the present concentration-dependent rate. This is a candidate kinetic sink rather than an assumed dominant outcome.

reactions.name: Competing ornithine delta-lactam formation during drying

conditions.other: Proposed dry-down screen: initial aqueous pH 5-9; ornithine 1-100 mM before evaporation; 12-72 h per drying episode, followed by rehydration. Track water activity and distinguish alpha-linked oligomers, branched products, and lactam. These are proposed conditions, not an assertion that the cited study used this entire range.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack of the delta-amine on the carboxyl group, with dehydration, forms a six-membered lactam.
reactions.reasoning: Frenkel-Pinter et al. (2019) experimentally identify ornithine lactamization as a competing process during prebiotic dry-down oligomerization. It therefore penalizes indiscriminate evaporation or an assumed ornithine-first peptide route. The cited result does not establish the lactamization rate in every aqueous or mineral-rich setting.

reactions.name: Competing alpha-amine guanidination of ornithine

conditions.other: Evaluate alongside rxn_021 at pH 8.5-10.5, ornithine 0.1-10 mM, cyanamide 5-100 mM, and 1-14 days. Determine alpha-versus-delta product ratios using structurally validated standards. Include further guanidination in the measured missing-product balance if it occurs.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-amine, rather than the delta-amine, attacks cyanamide to give a constitutional isomer of arginine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a quantified product channel under these conditions, but chemically necessary to test because free ornithine has two accessible amino groups. Longo et al. (2020) cannot establish free-monomer site selectivity from peptide experiments in which alpha-amines are largely tied up in amide bonds. The isomer is represented separately despite having the same formula as arginine.

reactions.name: Candidate arginine loss by hydrolytic deguanidination

conditions.other: Proposed product-survival assay: cooled-sample pH 10-11.5; authentic arginine 0.1-10 mM; sample over 1-90 days in the same matrix as rxn_017 and rxn_018. No nonzero rate is assumed. Measure ornithine and urea together and distinguish this channel from other thermal losses.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the guanidino carbon-nitrogen linkage yields ornithine and urea without invoking an enzyme.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative kinetic sink under the proposed conditions; no supplied study establishes its rate in this window. It is chemically justified as a product-survival test for prolonged alkaline processing. A formally possible endpoint hydrolysis cannot establish arginine accumulation unless product destruction is also constrained; this edge is not presented as an experimentally demonstrated arginase-like prebiotic cycle.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-stage guanidination with copper photoreduction and acidic finishing
pathways.description: Strongest literature-supported precursor scaffold. Immediate cyanamide interception follows copper-assisted aminonitrile reduction, then two homologation operations produce the characterized arginine alpha-aminonitrile. Acid hydration and amide hydrolysis are explicit, unvalidated finishing steps. No end-to-end free-arginine yield is established.

pathways.name: Early guanidination with copper photoreduction and acidic finishing
pathways.description: Branches through the relatively inefficient guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile before reduction. Measured flux through the early-guanylated nitrile is required; arginine precursor recovered from a mixed irradiation cannot automatically be assigned to this route. Shares the unresolved acidic finishing steps of P1.

pathways.name: Copper-depleted first photoreduction with aldehyde trapping and acidic finishing
pathways.description: Tests whether sulfide-only photochemistry can reduce the unguanidinated C3 nitrile after entry-stage copper is sequestered. This first reduction is substrate-specifically unvalidated; later copper-assisted steps remain, so the entire route is not copper-free. Acidic conversion to free arginine remains unverified.

pathways.name: Early guanidination with copper-depleted first photoreduction and acidic finishing
pathways.description: Combines inefficient early guanidination with a speculative sulfide-only reduction of its product. This is a lower-evidence candidate, not an experimentally demonstrated alternative. Remaining homologation chemistry follows the stronger scaffold, and terminal acidic hydrolysis still requires validation.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-stage guanidination with copper photoreduction and alkaline finishing
pathways.description: Uses the strongest precursor scaffold but transfers the aminonitrile to an alkaline hydrothermal compartment instead of an acidic one. Transfer recovery, nitrile hydration rate, amide cleavage, and arginine survival must all be measured. Geological alkalinity does not demonstrate selective completion.

pathways.name: Early guanidination with copper photoreduction and alkaline finishing
pathways.description: A conditional sequence requiring both productive early-guanylated nitrile flux and a selective alkaline endpoint. Neither efficient passage through the early branch nor accumulation of free arginine during prolonged alkaline processing is established by the supplied evidence.

pathways.name: Copper-depleted first photoreduction with aldehyde trapping and alkaline finishing
pathways.description: Tests two independent geological constraints: sequestration of entry copper and availability of alkaline rather than strongly acidic finishing fluids. The copper-free substrate reduction and alkaline hydrolysis are both hypotheses. Their combination does not gain experimental support merely from sharing demonstrated middle steps.

pathways.name: Early guanidination with copper-depleted first photoreduction and alkaline finishing
pathways.description: Lowest-evidence cyanosulfidic variant: inefficient early guanidination is followed by an unvalidated copper-free substrate reduction and an unvalidated alkaline endpoint. It is a distinct graph path and a conditional experimental hypothesis, not an established prebiotic synthesis.

pathways.name: Volcanic-discharge ornithine followed by free-monomer guanidination
pathways.description: Uses discharge-derived ornithine rather than assuming it is a cost-free feedstock. The source node is a coarse-grained mixture-production channel. Rainout recovery, free-versus-hydrolyzable ornithine, concentration, cyanamide availability, and delta-versus-alpha guanidination selectivity are unresolved. Peptide guanidination evidence is not substituted for free-monomer validation.

pathways.name: Heterogeneous CO/H2/NH3 ornithine followed by free-monomer guanidination
pathways.description: Uses the isotope-supported historical ornithine assignment, not the contested direct arginine assignment. The gas-solid source, cooling, extraction, and any precursor hydrolysis are coarse-grained and not established under the proposed hydrothermal interface conditions. Subsequent cyanamide guanidination retains the free-monomer site-selectivity and reagent-competition problems of P9.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest supported route in the submitted network. Aldehyde-stage cyanamide trapping and subsequent homologation follow the experimentally supported Patel et al. (2015) chemistry through the arginine alpha-aminonitrile. Acidic nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis are chemically conventional, but selective recovery of free arginine from this particular reaction mixture is not demonstrated. Rapid interception of the photogenerated aldehyde must be established rather than assuming a stable, transferable aldehyde inventory. Surface photochemistry followed by acidic thermal processing is not intrinsically inconsistent, but numerical operating conditions and a physical transfer protocol are absent.
suggestions: Demonstrate rxn_015 and rxn_016 with authenticated arginine alpha-aminonitrile, measuring argininamide, arginine, ornithine, and other degradation products over time.
Specify UV spectrum and dose, sulfide concentration, copper speciation, pH, temperature, and reagent-addition timing for the photochemical stages.
Run an integrated sequence with immediate aldehyde trapping and measured transfer recovery, rather than combining independently optimized step yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The reaction sequence is connected and chemically plausible, but direct beta-aminopropionitrile guanidination is specifically described as inefficient in the supplied Patel evidence. Residual aminonitrile and cyanamide can subsequently enter the aldehyde-trapping route, so an observed final product would not by itself establish that the early-guanidination sequence carried the productive flux. The acidic endpoint remains plausible but unvalidated for selective free-arginine recovery.
suggestions: Measure conversion and selectivity in rxn_005, including cyanamide hydrolysis and dimerization.
Track mol_011 during irradiation to distinguish rxn_005-to-rxn_006 flux from subsequent aldehyde-stage guanidination of residual starting material.
Establish acidic hydrolysis and arginine survival using the actual photochemical product mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Copper-free sulfide photochemistry is supported in parts of the broader literature, but that does not establish useful beta-aminopropionitrile-to-aldehyde conversion under the conditions needed here. Reaction rxn_007 is therefore a substantive substrate-specific experimental gap, not a conservation violation. This pathway still requires copper for rxn_001; copper depletion before the first photoreduction must be physically demonstrated. The downstream scaffold is well motivated, while free-arginine recovery remains unverified.
suggestions: Compare rxn_007 with rxn_003 using matched photon exposure, sulfide concentration, pH, and substrate concentration.
Measure residual copper and organic-material recovery after any proposed precipitation, sorption, or separation step.
Determine whether aldehyde production and immediate cyanamide capture outcompete substrate and reagent losses.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This variant combines inefficient early guanidination with an unestablished copper-free reduction of the guanidinated nitrile. General sulfide photoreactivity cannot substitute for evidence that mol_011 forms the intended aldehyde/hemiaminal selectively. The subsequent homologation sequence is coherent, and all reactions pass the supplied conservation check, but productive flux through the first two distinguishing steps is uncertain. Acidic finishing adds the same unresolved endpoint as P1.
suggestions: Test authenticated mol_011 directly under copper-depleted irradiation conditions and identify the product distribution.
Quantify early guanidination before attempting an integrated sequence, including the contribution of residual cyanamide to alternative productive chemistry.
Demonstrate copper depletion without assuming quantitative retention of the organic intermediates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route to the alpha-aminonitrile has the same strong literature basis as P1. Alkaline nitrile and amide hydrolysis are chemically possible, but no temperature-pH-residence-time window is supplied that establishes hydrolysis faster than loss of the guanidinated substrate or product. Reaction rxn_026 appropriately acknowledges one possible loss channel, but its inclusion does not establish a favorable kinetic window. The Hydrothermal label alone is insufficient to evaluate this finishing module.
suggestions: Measure competing rates of nitrile hydration, amide hydrolysis, and arginine degradation over an explicit alkaline temperature-pH matrix.
Benchmark alkaline finishing against acidic finishing using the same precursor mixture and analytical recovery procedure.
Specify pressure, residence time, quench conditions, and product recovery rather than assuming arginine accumulates in a continuously heated system.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a plausible connected candidate, but it combines the documented inefficiency of early guanidination with an unvalidated alkaline finishing module. Neither issue makes the reactions atomically impossible; both limit confidence that a useful inventory of free arginine survives the complete sequence. Residual reagents and products from rxn_005 must be included when evaluating subsequent irradiation and hydrolysis.
suggestions: Determine the actual mol_011 inventory and competing product inventory before irradiation.
Evaluate alkaline finishing on the crude upstream mixture as well as on purified alpha-aminonitrile.
Measure arginine loss independently so that transient formation is distinguished from recoverable target accumulation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Aldehyde-stage trapping is a sound strategic choice, but the route depends on both substrate-specific copper-depleted photoreduction and selective alkaline endpoint hydrolysis that are not established by the supplied evidence. The environmental concern is not the succession of surface and thermal settings; it is the absence of demonstrated copper depletion, intermediate recovery, and a target-preserving hydrolysis window.
suggestions: Validate rxn_007 independently before interpreting downstream negative or positive results.
Report copper speciation and recovery through depletion and transfer, including adsorption losses.
Establish a timed alkaline hydrolysis and quench protocol with quantitative arginine and degradation-product measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This variant has the greatest unresolved bottleneck burden among the scaffold pathways: inefficient early guanidination, unvalidated copper-free reduction of mol_011, and unvalidated alkaline recovery of free arginine. The central homologation chemistry remains literature-motivated, but successful operation of that module does not resolve the entry and finishing uncertainties. No conservation failure is identified.
suggestions: Establish product-specific conversion and selectivity for each distinguishing reaction before attempting the complete sequence.
Use copper-containing and aldehyde-stage-trapping controls to identify which chemistry actually carries productive flux.
Measure intermediate survival and target recovery under the proposed alkaline conditions rather than inferring them from formal hydrolysis stoichiometry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Volcanic-discharge chemistry provides evidence for an abiotic ornithine source, but rxn_019 is an aggregate product-source channel rather than a resolved selective synthesis. Its balanced equation does not establish the concentration or recovery of free ornithine available downstream. Cyanamide guanidination is mechanistically plausible, but delta-selectivity on free ornithine is not demonstrated by Longo et al.'s peptide experiments. The explicit alpha-guanylation, cyanamide-loss, and lactamization sinks are appropriate acknowledgments of competition, not evidence that the arginine-forming branch dominates.
suggestions: Quantify free ornithine in collected discharge products and distinguish it from ornithine released only during analytical workup.
Measure free-ornithine guanidination across defined pH and cyanamide concentrations, resolving arginine from N-alpha-guanylornithine.
Demonstrate rainout, collection, and concentration with measured recovery, including lactamization and cyanamide consumption where drying is used.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied isotope-confirmation literature supports ornithine from heterogeneous CO/H2/NH3 chemistry, so this pathway should not inherit the separate uncertainty surrounding the historical direct-arginine assignment. Nevertheless, rxn_020 remains a low-selectivity aggregate source with unresolved intermediates and recovery. The cited 200-700 degree Celsius mineral/gas experiments are not adequately specified by the Hydrothermal label: catalyst, phase, pressure, cooling, and collection must be distinguished. Downstream delta-selective cyanamide guanidination of free ornithine remains unvalidated.
suggestions: Specify whether rxn_020 represents a gas-solid reactor, a hot mineral interface, or an aqueous hydrothermal system, and justify any departure from the cited experiments.
Measure ornithine-specific production, release, survival during cooling, and downstream aqueous recovery rather than using total amino-acid yield.
Validate cyanamide guanidination on the recovered mixed product stream and distinguish arginine from constitutional isomers.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid and scientifically useful as a candidate experimental program, but it is not approved as a demonstrated complete synthesis network because confidence remains below 0.90. Its 28 molecule nodes and 26 reaction nodes form a connected network, molecule IDs are consistent, and the deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction: 17 are balanced as written and nine are balanceable with coefficients. There are no UNBALANCED reactions. Coefficients of eight associated with S8 are not intrinsically implausible. In rxn_012, H2S cancels in the displayed inferred balance; the formal sulfur bookkeeping should not be mistaken for a measured photochemical mechanism or sulfur-product distribution. Sink nodes and unspecified target stereochemistry are not defects. The principal strength is the literature-supported construction of the arginine alpha-aminonitrile, especially through aldehyde-stage cyanamide trapping. The submission correctly distinguishes this achievement from quantitative recovery of free arginine and does not misrepresent peptide guanidination as an environmental free-monomer experiment. However, all eight scaffold variants share an unvalidated finishing module, and both ornithine routes share unvalidated free-ornithine guanidination selectivity. Their enumeration does not provide independent confirmation of target achievement. Reactions rxn_022 and rxn_023 represent chemically reasonable cyanamide sinks; rxn_024 addresses literature-supported ornithine lactamization; rxn_025 acknowledges plausible competing alpha-guanylation; and rxn_026 identifies a possible arginine-loss channel. Their rates and importance under the proposed conditions remain unknown, and the literature-described unguanidinated/proline-precursor branch is not explicitly represented. Environmental assessment is limited because this representation supplies no numerical reaction windows, catalyst loadings, UV exposures, residence times, or concrete transfer protocols. Recovered moles divided by receiving volume is correct accounting, but it does not establish a physically viable transfer. Copper availability, sulfide concentration, UV penetration, and reagent sequencing require joint demonstration rather than separate assertions. Literature alignment is substantively good, although reaction-level citations and protocol mappings should be added, particularly for copper-free variants and the ornithine source channels. The decisive next result is an integrated experiment that establishes intermediate identities, resolves arginine from N-alpha-guanylornithine, measures transfer and competing-reaction losses, and quantifies recoverable free arginine.
